```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 6,
  out.width = "100%",
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

**HeatmapR** reads single-cell data where it lives, without converting it first. It reads `SingleCellExperiment` and `Seurat` objects, AnnData files, cytometry files and plain matrices, in memory or on disk. Features are chosen by name, groups and annotations come from the cells' metadata, and only the chosen features of the cells shown are ever made dense, so a few markers of a million cells need little memory.

This page covers the basics: what HeatmapR reads, heatmaps of cells and summaries of groups. Four guides go further:

- [Markers, dot plots and gene sets](markers.html): ranking the markers of each group, dot plots, gene-set scores, data sets side by side, and clusters that may be two populations.
- [Samples and conditions](conditions.html): the make-up of samples, pseudobulk tests between conditions with the samples as replicates, and plots that compare conditions within each cell type.
- [Cytometry](cytometry.html): flow and mass cytometry events, the asinh transform and quantile scaling, cluster medians and abundances, and differential states.
- [Trajectories](trajectories.html): genes smoothed along pseudotime, lineages side by side, and cells ordered without a pseudotime.

```{r}
library(HeatmapR)
```

## What HeatmapR reads

| Data | Features | Values (`assay`) | Metadata (`group_by`, `annotation_by`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SingleCellExperiment`, `SummarizedExperiment` | row names, or gene symbols in `rowData()` | an assay: `"logcounts"` by default, else `"exprs"`, else the first | columns of `colData()` |
| `Seurat` (`Assay` and `Assay5`) | row names of the assay | the `"data"` layer of the default assay, another layer (`"counts"`, `"scale.data"`), another assay (`"ADT"`) or both (`c("ADT", "data")`) | columns of `meta.data` |
| AnnData (`.h5ad`), with `heat_map_read_h5ad()` | the index of `var`, or a column of symbols or IDs | `X`, a layer, or `raw` | columns of `obs` |
| `DelayedArray` assays (HDF5Array, TENxMatrix), BPCells layers | as above | read a block of features at a time | as above |
| `flowFrame`, `flowSet` (flowCore not needed) | marker names (`desc`, e.g. `"CD3"`) or channels (`"FL1-A"`) | the intensities | columns of a `flowFrame`, `"sample"` and `pData()` of a `flowSet` |
| Sparse matrices (`dgCMatrix`), one cell per row (`t()` of a genes-by-cells matrix) | column names | the values | vectors of one value per cell |
| Matrices and data frames, one cell per row | column names | the values | columns of the data (left out of the features) or vectors |

Cells are drawn as rows and features as columns, as in scanpy and cytometry, and `swap_axes = TRUE` gives Seurat's layout of genes as rows. A handful of arguments do most of the work, in `heat_map()`, `heat_map_summarise()`, `heat_map_dot()` and the other functions of these guides:

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `features` | the genes, proteins or markers to show, by name, or a named list of groups of them |
| `assay` | which values: an assay of a `SingleCellExperiment`, an assay or layer of a `Seurat` object, a layer of an AnnData file |
| `group_by` | a metadata column (or vector) grouping the cells, e.g. clusters or cell types; several columns for their combinations, e.g. cell type and condition |
| `group_max` | the most cells to show from each group, so small groups stay visible |
| `annotation_by` | metadata columns drawn as annotation tracks |
| `swap_axes` | features as rows and cells as columns |
| `transform`, `cofactor` | the asinh transform of cytometry intensities |

## Example data

`heat_map_example()` simulates the data of these guides. `"rna"` gives 3,000 peripheral blood cells of six types from four donors in two conditions, with 2,000 genes, four of them markers of each cell type. As a `SingleCellExperiment`, the counts and log-normalised counts (`logcounts`) are sparse matrices with genes as rows and cells as columns, the cells' metadata is in `colData()` and the markers of each type are in `metadata()`. Without `class`, it gives the same cells as a data frame, one row per cell, which every function here reads too. `"cytometry"` and `"trajectory"` simulate the data of the [cytometry](cytometry.html) and [trajectory](trajectories.html) guides.

```{r data}
library(SingleCellExperiment)
sce <- heat_map_example("rna", class = "SingleCellExperiment")
sce
markers <- metadata(sce)$markers
markers
head(colData(sce))
```

## A heatmap of cells

`features` chooses the genes and `group_by` groups the cells by a column of `colData()`. The groups are separated and labelled in the order of their levels.

```{r cells, fig.alt = "Heatmap of 3,000 simulated cells by 24 marker genes, the cells grouped by cell type into six labelled blocks, each with its four marker genes high."}
heat_map(
  sce,
  features = unlist(markers),
  group_by = "cell_type",
  axis_text_y = NA,
  title = "Marker genes in 3,000 cells"
)
```

Only the 24 chosen genes of the cells shown are read from the sparse matrix, in compiled code; the other 1,976 genes are never touched. A missing feature is an error that names it, and a message warns when the dense values would take more than 1 GB.

### Downsampling and annotations

Large groups crowd out small ones. `group_max` keeps at most that many cells of each group, drawn with a fixed seed by `heat_map_downsample()`, and every cell of smaller groups. `annotation_by` draws metadata columns as tracks beside the cells.

```{r downsample, fig.alt = "Heatmap of at most 100 cells of each of the six cell types by 24 marker genes, grouped and labelled by cell type, with annotation tracks for sample and condition on the right."}
heat_map(
  sce,
  features = unlist(markers),
  group_by = "cell_type",
  group_max = 100,
  annotation_by = c("sample", "condition"),
  axis_text_y = NA,
  title = "At most 100 cells of each type"
)
```

`heat_map_downsample()` gives the same cells, for other plots and analyses:

```{r downsample-counts}
keep <- heat_map_downsample(sce$cell_type, n = 100)
table(sce$cell_type[keep])
```

### Genes as rows

`swap_axes = TRUE` draws genes as rows and cells as columns, as Seurat's `DoHeatmap()` does, with the groups and annotations along the top. A named list of features groups the genes too.

```{r swap, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Heatmap with 24 marker genes as rows, grouped and labelled by the cell type they mark, and cells as columns, grouped by cell type along the top, at most 100 cells of each type; the high values form a block diagonal."}
heat_map(
  sce,
  features = markers,
  group_by = "cell_type",
  group_max = 100,
  swap_axes = TRUE,
  axis_text_x = NA,
  title = "Genes as rows"
)
```

### Ordering the cells

Within each group the cells keep their order in the data. `tree_order_y = "spectral"` orders them so that similar cells sit together, without a dendrogram (see the [ordering guide](ordering.html)); `tree_y = TRUE` clusters them within each group instead, and `tree_kmeans_y` splits cells without groups into k-means clusters. The [large heatmaps guide](large-data.html) shows how 100,000 rows are clustered in about a second. Here the cells are ordered within each type and the genes clustered:

```{r cells-ordered, fig.alt = "Heatmap of at most 100 cells of each cell type by 24 marker genes, grouped by cell type, with the cells ordered within each group so that cells in which the same markers are detected sit together, and the genes clustered by a dendrogram along the top, so each type's four markers sit together."}
heat_map(
  sce,
  features = unlist(markers),
  group_by = "cell_type",
  group_max = 100,
  tree_order_y = "spectral",
  tree_x = TRUE,
  axis_text_y = NA,
  title = "Cells ordered within each type"
)
```

## Seurat objects, AnnData files and data on disk

### Seurat objects

A `Seurat` object is read the same way, from its default assay's `"data"` layer (or the assay or layer given to `assay`, e.g. `"counts"`, `"scale.data"` or `c("ADT", "data")`), with groups and annotations from `meta.data`. Layers split by sample are joined first with `SeuratObject::JoinLayers()`.

```{r seurat, fig.width = 9, fig.alt = "The same genes-as-rows heatmap drawn from a Seurat object holding the simulated data, grouped by cell type."}
library(SeuratObject)
seu <- suppressWarnings(CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = counts(sce),
  meta.data = as.data.frame(colData(sce))
))
seu <- SetAssayData(seu, layer = "data", new.data = logcounts(sce))
heat_map(
  seu,
  features = markers,
  group_by = "cell_type",
  group_max = 100,
  swap_axes = TRUE,
  axis_text_x = NA,
  title = "From a Seurat object"
)
```

Seurat's `DoHeatmap()` shows the z-scores of the `"scale.data"` layer by default; `assay = "scale.data"` reads that layer, and `scale = "row"` with `scale_method = "zscore"` scales the genes of the `"data"` layer as it is drawn here.

### AnnData files

AnnData (`.h5ad`) files written by scanpy and anndata, or downloaded from CELLxGENE, are read by `heat_map_read_h5ad()` without Python, through the hdf5r package. The metadata of the cells (`obs`) is read at once, so `group_by` and `annotation_by` name its columns. `X`, a layer (`assay = "counts"`) or `raw` is read as a sparse matrix the first time it is used and kept for the next heatmap. Features are named by the index of `var` or by a column of symbols or IDs, such as CELLxGENE's `feature_name`. A small file of 60 cells of three types comes with the package:

```{r h5ad, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3, fig.alt = "Dot plot of eight genes in three cell types read from an AnnData file. The first four genes are large dark red dots in T cells and small elsewhere."}
file <- system.file("extdata", "example.h5ad", package = "HeatmapR")
cells <- heat_map_read_h5ad(file)
cells
dot <- heat_map_dot(cells, features = paste0("GENE", 1:8), group_by = "cell_type",
                    title = "From an AnnData file")
```

The name of the file can also be given to any function, e.g. `heat_map_dot("pbmc.h5ad", ...)`, which reads it each time.

### Data on disk

Assays too large for memory can stay on disk. A `SingleCellExperiment` whose assays are `DelayedArray` objects - e.g. written with HDF5Array's `writeHDF5Array()` or `writeTENxMatrix()`, or loaded with `HDF5Array::loadHDF5SummarizedExperiment()` - and a `Seurat` object whose layers are BPCells matrices are read like those in memory. Heatmaps and dot plots read only the chosen features of the cells shown. Summaries, markers and scores of every gene read the data a block of genes at a time, each block realised as a sparse (or dense) matrix and passed to the same compiled code, so the results are the same as those of the data in memory. (A `DelayedArray` that only wraps a matrix in memory is read as that matrix.) Here the logs of the counts are left as a delayed operation, which is read in blocks like data on disk:

```{r on-disk}
disk <- sce
assay(disk, "log1p") <- log1p(DelayedArray::DelayedArray(counts(sce)))
class(assay(disk, "log1p"))
memory <- sce
assay(memory, "log1p") <- log1p(counts(sce))
all.equal(
  heat_map_markers(disk, group_by = "cell_type", assay = "log1p"),
  heat_map_markers(memory, group_by = "cell_type", assay = "log1p")
)
```

```{r on-disk-hdf5, eval = FALSE}
# AN HDF5-BACKED OBJECT, SAVED ONCE AND LOADED WITHOUT READING THE COUNTS
HDF5Array::saveHDF5SummarizedExperiment(sce, "pbmc_h5")
disk <- HDF5Array::loadHDF5SummarizedExperiment("pbmc_h5")
heat_map_summarise(disk, group_by = "cell_type")
```

A block holds 2^24 values of all the cells (128 MB as a dense matrix) or eight times as many values of sparse data; `options(HeatmapR.block_values = )` sets the size.

## Summaries of groups

`heat_map_summarise()` reduces the cells of each group to one row: the mean, median, sum, number or proportion detected, or any function, of each feature. For sparse data the mean, sum, number, proportion detected and median are found from the non-zero values in compiled code, without a dense copy of the data, and equal those of the dense data exactly.

```{r summarise, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the mean log-normalised expression of 24 marker genes in each of the six cell types, scaled within each gene, with the cell types and genes clustered by dendrograms."}
means <- heat_map_summarise(sce, features = unlist(markers), group_by = "cell_type")
dense <- heat_map_summarise(
  as.matrix(Matrix::t(logcounts(sce)[unlist(markers), ])),
  group_y = sce$cell_type
)
# THE SAME NUMBERS ([, ] DROPS THE NUMBER OF CELLS IN EACH GROUP, WHICH THE
# SUMMARY OF group_by ALSO KEEPS)
identical(means[, ], dense)
heat_map(means, scale = "column", tree = "both",
         title = "Mean expression of each cell type")
```

The summary keeps the number of cells of each group in its `"n"` attribute, which `bar_values_y = "n"` draws as bars beside the groups:

```{r summarise-n, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "The heatmap of mean marker expression in six cell types, with bars beside the rows of the number of cells of each type, from about 160 dendritic cells to about 930 CD4 T cells."}
attr(means, "n")
heat_map(means, scale = "column", tree = "both", bar_values_y = "n",
         title = "Mean expression and the number of cells")
```

### Pseudobulk

Several columns in `group_by` give one row per combination, e.g. the summed counts of each cell type in each donor, the pseudobulk of differential expression. The summary keeps the metadata that is the same for every cell of each row, here the donor's condition (its `"groups"` attribute), so `heat_map()` can group and annotate the rows by it. [Samples and conditions](conditions.html) tests these sums between conditions.

```{r pseudobulk, fig.height = 7, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the summed counts of 24 marker genes in each cell type of each of four donors, as log2 counts per million, scaled within each gene, grouped by cell type in labelled strips and annotated by donor and condition. The four donors of each type look alike."}
pseudobulk <- heat_map_summarise(sce, features = unlist(markers), assay = "counts",
                                 group_by = c("cell_type", "sample"), fun = "sum")
dim(pseudobulk)
head(attr(pseudobulk, "groups"))
logcpm <- log2(pseudobulk / rowSums(pseudobulk) * 1e6 + 1)
heat_map(logcpm, scale = "column", group_by = "cell_type",
         annotation_by = c("sample", "condition"), axis_text_y = NA,
         title = "Pseudobulk of each cell type in each donor")
```

(The counts per million here are of the 24 genes shown; a full pseudobulk sums every gene, `features = NULL`.)

## Seurat and scanpy equivalents

The functions of Seurat (Hao et al. 2024), scanpy (Wolf, Angerer and Theis 2018; `sc.` functions) and Bioconductor that each function stands in for:

| To draw or compute | HeatmapR | Seurat, scanpy and Bioconductor |
|---|---|---|
| a heatmap of cells | `heat_map()` | `DoHeatmap()`; `sc.pl.heatmap()` |
| a dot plot | `heat_map_dot()` | `DotPlot()`; `sc.pl.dotplot()` |
| a heatmap of group means | `heat_map_summarise()`, then `heat_map()` | `AverageExpression()`; `sc.pl.matrixplot()`; scater's `plotGroupedHeatmap()` |
| the distribution of each gene in each group | `cell_values` of `heat_map()` | `VlnPlot()`; `sc.pl.stacked_violin()` |
| pseudobulk sums | `heat_map_summarise(fun = "sum")` | `AggregateExpression()`; scuttle's `aggregateAcrossCells()` |
| markers of each group | `heat_map_markers()` | `FindAllMarkers()`; `sc.tl.rank_genes_groups()`; scran's `scoreMarkers()` |
| a dot plot of markers | `heat_map_dot(markers)` | `sc.pl.rank_genes_groups_dotplot()` |
| gene-set scores | `heat_map_score()` | `AddModuleScore()`; `sc.tl.score_genes()` |
| a pseudobulk test between conditions | `heat_map_contrast()` | `FindMarkers()` on `AggregateExpression()`; decoupler and pyDESeq2; muscat |
| the cell types of each sample | `heat_map_composition()` | |
| genes along pseudotime | `heat_map_smooth()`, then `heat_map()` | `sc.pl.paga_path()` |
| a few cells of each group | `heat_map_downsample()`, `group_max` | `subset(downsample = )`; `sc.pp.subsample()` (of all cells) |

A few settings match the others' defaults:

- `swap_axes = TRUE` draws genes as rows, as `DoHeatmap()` does.
- `heat_map_dot()` z-scores the means as `DotPlot()` does; `scale = "range"` scales them as scanpy's `standard_scale = "var"`, and `scale = "none"` shows the means, as scanpy does by default.
- `heat_map_markers()` scores markers by their AUC with Wilcoxon p-values, as `sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(method = "wilcoxon")` and presto do.
- `heat_map_score(method = "module")` computes the score of `AddModuleScore()` and `sc.tl.score_genes()`.
- `cell_values = heat_map_summarise(..., fun = "values")` draws a density of each group's values inside each cell of a heatmap of group summaries (see the [cytometry guide](cytometry.html#distributions-behind-the-medians)).

Each draws on a heatmap, so every option of `heat_map()` (dendrograms, annotations, bars, labels of a few rows, zoom panels, legends and styles) can be added, and the figure can be described for screen readers with `heat_map_describe()`.

## Interactive pages and the app

`heat_map_html()` writes any of these plots to a web page: hovering over a cell shows its group, feature and values, clicking or dragging selects rows and columns (e.g. the genes of a cluster), and the selection can be copied or downloaded. Here is the dot plot of the AnnData file:

```{r html}
page <- heat_map_html(dot, title = "Dot plot of an AnnData file", height = 3)
page
```

`heat_map_app(sce)` opens an app to build heatmaps and dot plots of single-cell data in the browser, choosing the features, groups and annotations from lists, and writes the R code of the figure; see [Building heatmaps in the browser](app.html).

## Speed

```{r speed-setup, include = FALSE}
sc <- utils::read.csv("single-cell-benchmarks.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sc_info <- readLines("single-cell-benchmarks-info.txt")
sc_info <- stats::setNames(sub("^[^:]*: ", "", sc_info), sub(":.*", "", sc_info))
sc$size <- paste(format(sc$cells, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "cells x",
                 format(sc$genes, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "genes")
sc_summary <- function(task) {
  r <- sc[sc$task == task, ]
  key <- paste(r$method, r$size, sep = "\r")
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(r, factor(key, levels = unique(key))), function(z) {
    ok <- z$status == "ok"
    data.frame(method = z$method[1], size = z$size[1],
               n = as.numeric(z$cells[1]) * z$genes[1],
               seconds = if(any(ok)) stats::median(z$seconds[ok]) else NA,
               peak_mb = if(any(ok)) max(z$peak_mb[ok]) else NA,
               status = if(any(ok)) "ok" else z$status[1])
  }))
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}
sc_table <- function(task, value = c("time", "memory"), caption = NULL) {
  value <- match.arg(value)
  s <- sc_summary(task)
  sizes <- unique(s$size[order(s$n)])
  methods <- unique(s$method)
  tab <- sapply(methods, function(m) {
    z <- s[s$method == m, ][match(sizes, s$size[s$method == m]), ]
    v <- if(value == "time") {
      ifelse(z$status == "ok",
             ifelse(z$seconds < 10, sprintf("%.2f", z$seconds), sprintf("%.0f", z$seconds)),
             z$status)
    } else {
      ifelse(z$status != "ok", z$status,
             ifelse(z$peak_mb < 0.5, "< 1", format(round(z$peak_mb), big.mark = ",")))
    }
    v[is.na(z$method)] <- ""
    v
  })
  tab <- matrix(tab, nrow = length(sizes), dimnames = list(sizes, methods))
  knitr::kable(tab, align = "r", caption = caption)
}
# THE RANGE OF THE RATIOS OF THE TIMES OF TWO METHODS OVER THE SIZES
sum_ratio <- function(a, b, task = "summarise") {
  s <- sc_summary(task)
  sa <- s[s$method == a, ]
  r <- sa$seconds / s$seconds[s$method == b][match(sa$size, s$size[s$method == b])]
  paste(sprintf("%.1f", range(r)), collapse = " to ")
}
sc_get <- function(task, method, size, value = "seconds") {
  s <- sc_summary(task)
  s[[value]][s$method == method & s$size == size][1]
}
```

The single-cell functions were timed against their counterparts in Seurat `r sc_info[["Seurat"]]`, scran `r sc_info[["scran"]]` and scuttle `r sc_info[["scuttle"]]` on simulated counts of 12 cell types (10 marker genes each, about 10% of the other genes' values non-zero), log-normalised and held as sparse matrices with genes as rows, as each package stores them. Each case ran in a fresh R process on the machine of the [speed comparison](benchmarks.html) (`r sc_info[["cores"]]` cores, `r sc_info[["memory_gb"]]` GB), three times when it took less than 30 seconds, and the median is shown; runs were stopped after 10 minutes. Memory is the growth of the process's resident memory during the run, with the data already loaded.

In short:

- **Markers.** `heat_map_markers()` ranked the markers of 12 groups in 20,000 cells and 20,000 genes in `r round(sc_get("markers", "HeatmapR", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes"), 2)` seconds, where scran took `r round(sc_get("markers", "scran (scoreMarkers)", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes"))` to `r round(sc_get("markers", "scran", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes"))` seconds and Seurat `r round(sc_get("markers", "Seurat", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes"))` seconds and `r format(round(sc_get("markers", "Seurat", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes", "peak_mb") / 1000, 1))` GB. Like Seurat, HeatmapR scores only the features that pass its filters, one group against the rest; scran's functions compute statistics for every gene between every pair of groups, which takes longer and tells you more.
- **Summaries.** scuttle's `summarizeAssayByGroup()` was the fastest at the mean and proportion detected of every gene, `r sum_ratio("HeatmapR", "scuttle")` times as fast as `heat_map_summarise()` (which makes one pass for each), and Seurat's `AverageExpression()` took `r sum_ratio("Seurat", "HeatmapR")` times as long as HeatmapR, with up to `r format(round(max(sc_summary("summarise")$peak_mb[sc_summary("summarise")$method == "Seurat"]) / 1000, 1))` GB of memory. For a heatmap or dot plot only the chosen features are summarised.
- **Plots.** A dot plot of 40 genes in 100,000 cells took `r round(sc_get("dotplot", "HeatmapR", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes"), 2)` seconds against `r round(sc_get("dotplot", "Seurat", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes"), 1)` for Seurat's `DotPlot()`, and a heatmap of the 40 genes in every one of the 100,000 cells `r round(sc_get("heatmap", "HeatmapR", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes"), 1)` seconds against `r round(sc_get("heatmap", "Seurat", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes"))` seconds and `r format(round(sc_get("heatmap", "Seurat", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes", "peak_mb") / 1000, 1))` GB for `DoHeatmap()`.

**Markers of every group against the other cells**: `heat_map_markers(sce, group_by = "group")`, scran's `scoreMarkers()` (AUCs and other effect sizes between every pair of groups) and `findMarkers(test.type = "wilcox", direction = "up")` (Wilcoxon tests between every pair of groups), and Seurat's `FindAllMarkers(only.pos = TRUE, min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.25)` (one-vs-rest Wilcoxon tests`r if(sc_info[["presto"]] == "FALSE") ", without the presto package, which Seurat uses to speed them up when it is installed"`). Times in seconds:

```{r speed-markers, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("markers")
```

Peak memory in MB:

```{r speed-markers-memory, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("markers", "memory")
```

**Mean and proportion detected of every gene in every group** (pseudobulk): `heat_map_summarise()` (twice, once for each), scuttle's `summarizeAssayByGroup(statistics = c("mean", "prop.detected"))` and Seurat's `AverageExpression()`. Times in seconds:

```{r speed-summarise, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("summarise")
```

**A dot plot of 40 genes** (`heat_map_dot()` and Seurat's `DotPlot()`) and **a heatmap of 40 genes in every cell**, grouped (`heat_map(swap_axes = TRUE)` and Seurat's `DoHeatmap()`), drawn to a PNG file. Times in seconds:

```{r speed-plots, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("dotplot", caption = "Dot plot")
sc_table("heatmap", caption = "Heatmap")
```

Peak memory of the heatmaps in MB:

```{r speed-heatmap-memory, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("heatmap", "memory")
```

The scripts are in [`data-raw/benchmarks`](https://github.com/DillonHammill/HeatmapR/tree/master/data-raw/benchmarks): `single-cell-case.R` runs one case and `single-cell-run.R` runs them all and writes `vignettes/articles/single-cell-benchmarks.csv`, which this page reads.

## References

Hao, Y. et al. (2024). Dictionary learning for integrative, multimodal and scalable single-cell analysis. *Nature Biotechnology*, 42(2), 293-304. [doi:10.1038/s41587-023-01767-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-023-01767-y)

Wolf, F. A., Angerer, P. and Theis, F. J. (2018). SCANPY: large-scale single-cell gene expression data analysis. *Genome Biology*, 19, 15. [doi:10.1186/s13059-017-1382-0](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-017-1382-0)
